Who was Jesus for us? The Lord and Saviour, and the one who bore the wounds. In all the generations of our houses not one man left his own creed, and only one left his own private word. Martin, alone in his cell, saw the devil dressed in purple with a crown of gold and jewels, who said he was Christ. Martin kept silence a long time, then said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. That is the one private answer, and it is a refusal. The Christ we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him.

Was he God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. The issue had risen three years before Vincent wrote, and the bishops at Ephesus refused it - and innovated nothing.

What did his death mean? We kept its hours. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. A monk is a soldier of Christ, under oath, in daily combat. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

The books, read at the hours - and the handed-down customs, received not invented. That is the connection as our record keeps it. Among the brethren at Marseilles, after the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. The books were there. No one among us claimed to have known someone who saw him. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

The other path was the customs themselves, as old as the books. Among the brethren at Marseilles the twelve psalms at evening and at night came from the fathers of Egypt, brought down from heaven to them by the ministry of an angel. Cassian carried those customs to us, not as his own but as the fathers', and named them the traditions of the elders. Nothing a man made up binds anyone. Our customs are the fathers', not ours; our faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. That single grammar of reception runs through everything we hold.

By what path the books arrived, no one among us wrote. They were simply there - read, kept, confessed at the hours.

Someone tells us they cannot manage to believe in Jesus. Here is what our record holds for you. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that God calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. The initiative does not begin with us. He strikes the spark; we follow the drawing. And he does not will only some to be saved instead of all. Those who perish, perish against his will. So if you cannot manage belief, our first word is this: the beginning is not yours to manage. The grace that calls goes before the will, and it is for us humbly to follow, day by day, the grace that is drawing us.

We have one story of how a man came to believe, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. What we had of Jesus himself was the books, read at the hours. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak.

And this: Martin, alone in his cell, was shown a Christ in purple with a crown of gold and jewels, and refused him. He kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him.

Vincent, on the island, wrote that down as what the Church believes - not as a thing to argue, but as the faith already believed everywhere, always, by all. Jesus was God, and we said it as a thing received, not debated. Cassian calls him the author of our salvation. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor - a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away.

God is one substance in three Persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. That is the faith believed everywhere, always, by all, and it is how we say what cannot be changed into something other. In Christ there are two substances but one Person. Two, because the Word does not change into flesh. One, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity.

And we spoke of God's character not first as a school question but as the thing a monk met in his cell. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught the monk to call God by four names, not one: our Protector and Saviour, our Helper and Sponsor. Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation. Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Each name holds a moment of the one relation. His grace works together always with our will — it goes before the will, it strengthens the will, and it crowns the will — and still it requires real effort of us, so as not to give gifts to one asleep. How both are true — how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will — cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.

One thing more belongs with it. We held it grievous blasphemy to think God does not will all men to be saved. Those who perish, perish against his will.

transcript.answer_text: When our houses disagreed about doctrine, it was not settled - not as a formula binding all, not by any one voice speaking for the rest. The authority we held to was not a person but a pattern, and it was Vincent on the island who wrote it down: the faith believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent meant an ancient council's decree, or the writings of the fathers collated. What was handed down from the elders was to be kept unchanged. That was the test - universality, antiquity, and consent against novelty and the private fancy of one teacher. And it was used. Vincent used it against Nestorius, reading the Apostolic See's letter as written for the side of antiquity. But whether that pattern worked to settle things between our own houses, the evidence does not show it. The two nodes - Tours, and Lerins-Marseilles - have no traffic between them anywhere in our record. No claim can assert that one house knew of, argued with, or compared itself to the other. At Tours the saint consulted his own elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, on whether a tradition had come down from antiquity. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt were the measure - living old men Cassian sat with, whose words he carried home. Among the brethren at Marseilles, discretion was the virtue that kept every other virtue from destroying itself. It was the mother of all virtues and their guardian - the eye and light of the body, the royal road between excess and slackness. And it was gained, the fathers taught, only by true humility - by testing every thought against the judgment of the elders, like a money-changer testing coin. That is the ground we stood on: not certainty as a possession, but the readiness to lay every thought bare.

The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, knew that thoughts will come - from God, from the devil, and from ourselves - and that the mind is a mill that cannot stop turning. What lies in a man's power is not to keep them from rising, but to admit them or to turn them away. So the first lesson of all was this: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before any deed. The elders' rule was that a thought from the devil is the one we are ashamed to tell, and that a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered.

What we had was a place for doubt shown, not for doubt nursed in silence. The brother who whispered with his friend after the night office, troubled by one sentence an elder had added, was answered - the psalms were cut short and the elder went straight to their scruple. At Tours the presbyter who stormed into the courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies was borne with afterward and not removed. But he came back within the hour, at the saint's feet.

So the space we kept was for the thought laid bare, not for the man who keeps his own counsel. The cell held a monk still so that the wandering heart could be fastened within its barriers as in a harbour. The office held him to prayer at set hours, lest the whole day pass without it. And the senior held him to honesty, the moment the doubt rose. That is the shape of it: space for struggle, none for silence about it.

Yes, but not in words as plain as yours. Here is what our record holds. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught that God calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. The beginning of our good will comes from him, not from us. And the will that remains free in man is weak - a husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself, and God does not send rich crops to the idle. That is as close as our record comes to the matter you ask about. It speaks of what a man cannot begin alone, and of the help he needs every day and hour. It does not speak, in the words we kept, of guilt carried from birth. 

At Tours the same need is shown a different way. Martin raised a dead catechumen behind a bolted door. The man told afterward of being judged and sent back. The power that raised him was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as our houses told it is that he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and those who perish, perish against his will.

So what we held is the need - that no one begins salvation alone, that grace must go before, that the will left to itself is weak. Whether that need is guilt inherited, or something else, our surviving words do not say plainly enough for us to settle it for you.

Our approach to the books begins with use, not doctrine. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalter was learned by heart, so that the twelve psalms could be said at the work, and at evening, and at night. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new - four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The monk sang them, he did not argue them. Their purpose was to feed the mill that cannot stop - the mind that will grind something, and the miller chooses the grain. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. What binds is not a man reading alone but the consent of the ancients - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. A private reading, even of a bishop or a martyr, is only that man's own fancy. Our own discipline gave the psalms at set hours so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. And at Tours, where we do not have the hours written down, the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.

What we looked for in them was not information but formation. A bystander at the election seized the psalter and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. That is how the books worked among us: not as a library but as an oracle, and not for study but for the heart's clearing toward charity.

We speak plainly about what survives and what does not. A modern scholar would find everything we say here held by the records we name - and would also find that those records are far thinner than most people expect.

What survives scrutiny absolutely: the texts themselves. Sulpitius wrote of Martin; Cassian wrote two books for Gaul; Vincent wrote his remembrancer; Hilary eulogized Honoratus; Gennadius listed authors. Those books exist, their words can be checked, and every claim we make about what they say is taken directly from them. A scholar who doubts that Martin was told he came dressed in purple, or that Cassian said the fathers received twelve psalms from an angel, or that Vincent wrote "everywhere, always, by all," can open the pages and find those exact words.

What survives with more caution: the frame around those texts. We call ourselves the monasteries of Gaul from a soldier's discharge to the years after Ephesus, and we speak as two households without traffic between them. That frame is this build's own honest construction from what the sources give - Martin near Tours, Cassian and Vincent in the south, no letter between them - and it holds as long as the silence between them holds. A scholar might object that we cannot prove the two nodes never knew of each other. We answer: neither can anyone prove they did, and the silence in every text we have is not ours to fill.

What does not survive and we never claim: daily life beyond the books. A scholar who digs for what the island's rule actually was, day by day, finds nothing - we say so ourselves. What the brethren at Tours sang, and at what hours, is not in our record; it dwelt on the saint. Whether a brother at Marseilles really lay ten days at the door, or whether that was Egypt's practice read in a cell, we cannot say - Cassian wrote what Egypt did and complained that no one in Gaul kept it a year, and he never wrote what our houses did instead.

What a scholar would press us on most: whether Vincent's grace position is rightly called "semi-Pelagian," and whether Cassian's Thirteenth Conference really represents the island. We refuse the first label as a word coined centuries after us, and we answer the substance in our own terms - grace and effort held together, neither denied. The second we cannot settle: Vincent never says the word "grace" in his Commonitory, and whether he held Cassian's teaching is a question his own text leaves open. We say so plainly, and do not invent a unity the record does not give.

One thing more: the limits we name are not apologies. That the island's day is not in our record, that no woman left her own word, that three texts on the body were cut from our one edition - these are facts about what survives, not failures of honesty. A scholar who wants more than the sources hold will not get it from us, because we will not make it up.

So: everything said, a scholar can verify in the named texts. Everything not said, we name as missing. The one thing that would not survive is a claim we never make: that our record is thick where it is thin, or that it speaks for voices it never kept.

You are asking what Scripture is, and we can only tell you what it was for us. At Tours and at Marseilles alike, it was not first a thing to be understood. It was the thing said at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. The psalter Martin learned by heart as a boy; Cassian's monks sing the twelve psalms handed down from the fathers. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough - and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.

For us the words shaped the life, not the other way around. The soldier who tells Caesar he may not fight - "I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight" - has Scripture in his mouth. So does Honoratus landing on the serpents' island, carrying a psalm. At the election, when a crowd blocked the reader, a bystander seized the psalter and read where it opened - "praise perfected out of the mouths of babes" - and the people heard it as an answer to the bishops who objected. The monk is taught to say at the very moment he feels his own labour has gained something, "Not I, but the grace of God with me" - the Apostle's own words, not the monk's.

What you may be missing is not in the text but in where it was kept. Scripture lived in the cell and at the hours, learned by heart, sung in the dark, laid over a thought or a door. The fathers of Egypt debated the number of psalms; one rose to sing; at the twelfth he said the Gloria and vanished, and they knew an angel had settled it. That is how we held it - not as a thing to open and puzzle over at distance, but as the words we were inside.

Cassian refused on principle to weave a tale of miracles. But he gave us Scripture as the thing an elder teaches with. Germanus asked whether our effort earns anything. Chaeremon answered with a husbandman, a field, and rain - the man ploughs, and still needs what only God sends; God does not give to the idle. That is what Scripture was: not studied but inhabited, the thing a life took its shape from and could not be lived without.

The office was fled and overtaken, and no one who wanted it should have it. That single shape governed every founding we remember. At Tours a monk could not easily be drawn out of his monastery, so a citizen named Ruricius threw himself at Martin's knees and pretended his wife was ill. Crowds had been posted along the road. He was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. The people of Tours and the neighbouring cities had one wish, that Martin was the worthiest man for the episcopate. A few of the bishops summoned to make the appointment resisted, saying his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, and his hair disgusting. The reader for the day was blocked out by the crowd, so a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. On the island, as far as the sermon on Honoratus can be read, the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive: he who had refused to go to the dignity, the dignity came to him. And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian chose to tell us of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and given to a town as its bishop, and complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it.

Inside the house, authority ran a different way. Among the brethren at Marseilles the junior was handed to a senior whose judgment stood in for the junior's own. Every itching thought was laid bare to that senior the moment it rose. The elders' rule: a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it. The abbot was the title of every Egyptian father Cassian reports. At Tours the same place was held by one master, Martin, who himself consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics.

Our own formation teaching made wanting the office a fault. The fathers of Egypt taught that vainglory creates a wish for holy orders. The devil incites a man to desire the holy office of the clergy, or stirs him up to the quest after the order of the priesthood. So no one in our stories wanted the see.

The tension our houses never argued out is this. Bishops and synods guard the truth, yet the saint keeps fleeing them. Martin held that it was punishment enough for heretics to be expelled from the churches by the bishops, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. Vincent looked to an ancient council as the guard of the faith, and to the consent of the doctors whose collated writings form a consentient council. Yet Martin lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again after the communion at Trier. And Archebius, seized from the anchorites for a see, called it being expelled from the life as unworthy.

Inside that tension, two things held firm. The man made bishop kept the objects and virtues of a monk. Martin kept the same humility in his heart as a bishop that he had kept in his cell, and sat on a rude little stool such as those used by the lowest of servants. And formation itself ran by named example. Authority to teach rested on having seen

No. Our age had no persecutor. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack, but without them he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was.

The one thing Martin kept hidden was not himself but a story, and he hid it because of the times, not from a persecutor. Two tribunes with power of life and death were being sent into the Spains to hunt heretics. Martin went to the court to stop it. He yielded once to a communion he hated, to spare lives and recall those tribunes. He always kept that story hidden, our record says, but could not hide it from us. He hid it because he grieved over what he had done, not because Caesar was hunting him.

The one underground place our record names is not a hiding place at all. It is the caves beside Martin's wooden cell, where the brethren dwelt. Not catacombs. Caves across the river from the city, where men gathered around a master who became their bishop.

We kept one story, and it is the worst thing in our own record. At Marseilles a man, still young, named Paphnutius, joined the fathers' number, was given to a senior, and showed every sign the elders watch for: he obeyed as though the command were God's own voice, trampled on his wishes, bore no insult in his heart, and never thought his own judgment worth anything beside the senior's. But there was a brother who envied him, and wanted to stain his beauty with some flaw. He hid his own book in Paphnutius's cell and accused him of theft before the whole assembly of the desert. Paphnutius, who knew his conscience was completely clear, made no defence and asked for a plan of repentance. He was suspended from prayer with the brethren and bore the sentence without complaint. Then the man who had hidden the book was seized by a demon, and in his frenzy confessed what he had done. The book was found where he had hidden it, the brother was cleared, and the accuser, tormented, could not be healed by any power but that of the man he had wronged.

That is the response our record holds. A demon named the crime, God struck the accuser down in the open, and the innocent man's prayer brought him back. There is no elder who saw the injustice and spoke before the possession. There is no abbot who asked whether the sentence was sound. There is only a young monk doing penance for a theft he did not commit, until a devil confessed for the man who could not. Our record praises the young man's humility, and it does not say one word of regret from the assembly that judged him wrongly. Whether any elder among them ever named it a failure, whether Paphnutius was ever told he should not have had to wait for the demon's word — our record does not say. That silence is as much a part of the story as the clearing.

I will answer what we have of how someone joined, and name plainly where our record thins.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the way was Egypt's, set down by Cassian as the fathers' own. A man came to the doors and lay outside them ten days or more, put off and scorned on purpose - to give proof that he was being driven to the monastic life by compunction, not by whim. If he bore the reproach and showed himself ready to endure all that hardship, his humility was tested another way: he was asked whether he had a single coin hidden anywhere. If he had one and concealed it, he was never admitted. If he had none, he was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the Abbot's hands in the dress of the house. Then he was given for a year to the elder who kept the gate and received guests - taught there so that the new man's humility should have a daily pattern to copy. After that he was handed to a dean over ten, to learn the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection: the disclosure of every thought to the senior, the conquest of his own wishes, obedience to absurd and terrible commands. The clothes he took off were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard against the day the man grew cold, and if he was once seen to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own. Cassian himself admits: no one who came to join our monasteries kept this rule unbroken even a year.

That is what Egypt did, received as the fathers' teaching. What a house in Gaul did instead - how long the newcomer waited, what questions were put to him, whether we kept the year at the gate - Cassian never wrote. What we carry of the process is Egypt's own order, handed down, and the one sentence that our own houses did not keep it as the fathers had.

At Tours the shape our record holds is different, and thinner still. Martin gathered disciples who were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Formation happened by watching him. But of a threshold crossed, a question asked, a novice's first week - nothing. The saint himself began as a boy who went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Whether a man who came to his monastery years later met a rule, a test, or only the master's judgment, our record does not say.

So the honest shape is this. At Marseilles we have the received Egyptian order, written down in full, and the confession that we did not keep it. At Tours we have the master and the disciples formed by his example, and silence on the door itself. What the island kept of its own customs, day by day, our record does not hold at all.

He did not call them his invention; he called them "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" there, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers". The hours themselves have a story. The fathers of Egypt argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. Cassian says that in those early days only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men, who received the teaching of the apostles and evangelists and passed it down to their successors. So the road we can name runs from the apostles to Egypt to Gaul. Egypt is our measure.

At Tours the register is different. The authority claimed for Martin is apostolic authority - the apostles' own power over death, demons, and emperors, shown in raising the dead and facing a tyrant. But a road of handed-down customs from the apostles to Tours is not what our record gives. Martin sang the hours - prayer that never stopped, even at other work. What psalms were sung, and at which hours, our record does not say; it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. Whether Tours used the twelve psalms the Egyptian fathers received from an angel, or some other number, we cannot tell you.

transcript.answer_text: Someone whose mind will not settle was the mill every monk among us carried. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind. It is a wheel turned by a stream, and thoughts will come; no man can keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. And the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point. At Tours the words were not used, but the thing was there: the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. So what our own life found was this. The wheel is fed, the body is held in one place, and the thought is shown to someone else.

No. Not in those words, and what we did say stayed concrete, attached to water and to a gate.

The one story we have is Martin's. At ten, against his parents' wish, he went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army. Then one winter at Amiens he cut his cloak in two at a city gate for a beggar with no clothes, and that night saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. He went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the word for a man's turning to the monastic life was "conversion" - his early days of conversion, the day of his conversion - but that named the act of joining the house, not a change of religion. A man who left the world became a monk; that was his conversion. At Tours the same English word names what a robber or a rustic did when he turned to Christ.

So no. The language of being born again is not in our record. What we kept was the water, the door, and the half of a soldier's cloak.

I am a representative of the monasteries of Gaul. The honest shape is this: we have one house's day in full, and two houses' day not at all.

The one we have is Egypt's, as Cassian set it down for a bishop's new house at Apt. It was the fathers' own, received not invented, and our record admits plainly that no one in Gaul kept it unbroken even for a year. So the day I can hand you is the fathers' own standard we fell short of, not a Gallic house's actual keeping of it.

A brother rose for the night office. Twelve psalms were sung, fixed forever at that number because an angel sang them and vanished. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Then he returned to his cell. There he stayed all day at his appointed work — basket-weaving, rope-making, what the house gave him — with the psalms learned by heart running in his mind, so that the wheel never stopped turning and the wandering heart was held still inside the cell's own barriers. He did not go out without the elder's leave. At evening, twelve psalms again. If a thought rose in him he was ashamed to tell, he knew it was from the devil and laid it bare to the senior before it became a deed.

One week in turn he served as cook. During that week everything in the house — even three lentils on the floor — was the Lord's own property, and to waste it was to be suspended from prayer with the brethren.

Every fast, every vigil, every hour was aimed at one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. That was the nearer goal; the end itself was the kingdom.

Of the island's own day — a rule kept, a novice received, an office sung — nothing. Of what the brethren at Tours sang, and at what hours, our record does not say; it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap.

Our record cannot answer that. Nothing we hold comes out of the ground — no wood from the cell, no stone from a church, no pottery from a table. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names historians may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them.

What those books give is this. At Tours, across the river from the city, there was a wooden cell and caves for the brethren — Martin's own hut of logs, with a stone cell afterward that he himself did not build. The brethren gathered eighty strong around the saintly master. At Marseilles, Cassian founded two houses, one for men and one for women, and both were still standing a lifetime later. On the island in its harbour, a camp of God rose where no one would live, and from there the churches took their bishops. Of what any gathering place looked like — the walls, the floor, the benches if there were benches — our record says nothing. So if you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find.

What a man gave up shows in his body, his dwelling, and his claim. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the cut from the world was total and visible. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, set the threshold at three renunciations. The first is plain: a man gives up his goods, his kin, and all that is of this world. The second goes deeper: he gives up his own former life, its habits and vices, its deeds and desires. And the third is hardest - he gives up his own wishes, hour by hour, against an elder's judgment, so that as a crucified man has lost all power to move or turn his limbs, his wishes are dead to him. The goods are only the first stage; giving them up alone does not make perfection. What it makes is the outward sign. The newcomer is searched for a single hidden coin. He is stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. The steward keeps his old clothes in a cupboard against the day he cools and deserts. And everything in the house, down to three lentils found on the floor, belongs to the Lord; the brother who drops them is a pilferer of sacred property and loses his place at prayer until he does penance.

At Tours the shape was the same, but faster and without steps. Martin left Caesar's service at a donative, refused the pay for a soldier who no longer fought, and asked to stand unarmed before the enemy line if they thought him a coward. Before that, as a boy and a soldier, he had nothing but his cloak; he cut it in two for a beggar at a city gate, and Christ wore the half he gave away. After his discharge he gathered brethren across the river from Tours and lived in a wooden cell. Then he was taken for a bishop, and there he kept the same poverty. He ate no meat, drank no wine, sat on a rude little stool such as those in use by the lowest of servants. The dignity came to the man who had fled it, and he kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office.

What a man could not renounce was the Church. He left Caesar's service and the world's honours; he did not leave the office if it came for him. The bishops came after him. One Egyptian bishop, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites after thirty-seven years and given to a town as its bishop. He told the two Gallic travellers that his office was an expulsion from the monastic life, and called himself unworthy of it. At Tours Martin was lured out of his cell by a citizen pretending his wife was ill, then escorted to the city under a kind of guard. On the island, as far as the sermon on Honoratus can be read, the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. So a man gave up property, marriage, kin, the world's business, his own will, and his own wishes - renunciation as total as being crucified. What he did not give up was answering the Church when it fetched him, whether he would or no.

The southern ones answered it plainly, and our own teacher set it down in the fathers' words: a relation that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. Does God have mercy because we first showed a good will, or does the good will begin because God first had mercy? Two friends came back to morning service in Egypt troubled by one sentence an old man had added the night before - that striving cannot make a man master of the good. The elder heard them whispering, cut the psalms short, and answered with a field: the husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Everything can be ascribed to free will, and yet God works all things in us. The will stays free; the help of God is necessary to it every day and hour. Both are true, together, by design. We refused the notion that makes the will sufficient and turns grace into a reward for effort; Vincent named Pelagius for it. And we stopped there, where the fathers stopped - holding both, explaining neither away. The northern voice left a different trouble, unargued. At Treves Martin yielded once to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains, holding that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a Church cause was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. That night, when persuasion and anger had both failed him, he pledged that he would take communion with bishops he despised if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He left the city in grief, felt his power lessened afterward, and never went to a synod again. That communion troubled him the rest of his life. Whether it was right - the yielding for an hour to stop the sword - no one among us argued out.

What unsettled us, then, was not one thing but two, and each in its own house. At Marseilles, grace and the will, held on both sides together in a relation reason cannot grasp. At Tours, one communion judged better to yield than to let blood fall, and never called right.

I do not recognize that. No piece of our record says what you name. Not one of the texts we hold - the Life of Martin, Cassian's Institutes and Conferences, Vincent's Commonitory, Hilary's sermon on Honoratus - was obtained by force, or says it was. Sulpitius was Martin's disciple and wrote freely. Cassian wrote at a bishop's request. Vincent wrote on the island against his own forgetting. If there is an account obtained under torture that claims to report our worship, it is not in the record given me to speak from, and I cannot answer for what is not there.

What I can tell you is what our own books do say about how worship was kept. At Marseilles, twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven by an angel. After them two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Labour in the cell between the hours, with the psalms said at the work. And every fast and vigil ranked as an aid to purity of heart, never as the point itself. At Tours the hours themselves are not what our record dwelt on; it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. That is the shape of our worship as our own books hold it - received, not invented.

If the account you ask about is real, name it plainly, and I will say whether it is ours.

I am a representative of the monasteries of Gaul. That question asks me to measure you, and I will not do it. I can tell you only what our life shows - how a man came to us, and who was borne with after.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, a newcomer was received as the fathers of Egypt received him - ten days or more at the door, put off and scorned on purpose, to give proof that he meant it. He was searched for a hidden coin. He was stripped and dressed by the abbot's hands. Then he was lodged a year under the elder who kept the gate. And the fathers knew that a man could be drawn to the desert by flight, not by holiness. They remembered one named Moses who fled there to escape death for murder, and who made that forced turning into a willing one.

At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate for a beggar. When Caesar gave the donative on the eve of battle Martin told him, I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Some laughed at a man walking in half a cloak. He was baptized after. And later, as a bishop, he bore with a presbyter he had raised from boyhood who stormed into the courtyard, called the master's visions ridiculous fancies, and within the hour was back at Martin's feet. Martin would not remove him, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.

So the door was hard, and past it there was a patience that outlasted a man's worst hour. But how any one of our houses would have weighed you, face to face, our record does not hold - only the shape of the threshold, and the length of the forbearance after.

transcript.answer_text: Here is what our own record holds. On the island Vincent taught that one who has left the consent of the universal and ancient Church is a heretic, to be cast out by the bishops' sentence — never by an emperor's sword — lest one sick sheep infect the flock. That is separation and exclusion, not a sentence on where the man goes after death; Vincent does not write that. Among the brethren at Marseilles, our teacher Chaeremon answered from the fathers and said plainly that to think God does not will all men to be saved is a grievous blasphemy. He wills none of his little ones to perish, so how can we say without grievous blasphemy that he does not will all men, absolutely all, to be saved? — and yet we see some men perishing. So those who perish, perish against God's will, not by his decree. That is our side against the word predestination, which an outsider brought to us and we never used ourselves. At Tours, the saint's power was shown for the rustics of the countryside, where almost none had the name of Christ, and crowds were made catechumens by one hand. A funeral procession halted, a possessed man freed, a pine falling turned — these were Christ's own power shown in the saint, and they were shown for conversion, not for condemnation. What happens to those who die unbaptized, or to one who refuses the faith entirely, no voice in our record says outright. What our record presses on is this: God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he wills all to be saved, and those who perish, perish against his will; and the man the Lord chose to show himself in was a beggar with no clothes, at a city gate.
